claims.claim: Dyson Logos, citing Decker and Noonan's 2005 GenCon table observations, holds that a DM gets two sentences before players stack dice; players missed dimensions, exits and monster counts in longer boxed text.
claims.source: Dyson's Dodecahedron — The Dreaded Boxed Text (Dyson Logos, 2013-09-29)

claims.claim: A 2025 EN World poster re-cites the 2005 Noonan/Decker WotC article: two sentences, 'DMs who didn't used boxed text had more engagement', cold reading is worse than personal phrasing, 'Ditch the boxed text and use your own words' — upstream article not fetched, single-lineage claim.
claims.source: EN World — Read aloud text in modules: What are folks' opinions? (thread, page 4, 2025-04-05)
claims.quote: Ditch the boxed text and use your own words

claims.claim: Thread posters set ceilings of 'no more than two sentences' (GM Lent) or '3 to 5 sentences at most' with listed details for closer investigation (el-remmen).
claims.source: EN World — Read aloud text in modules: What are folks' opinions? (thread, page 4, 2025-04-05)

claims.claim: Shawn Merwin's D&D Beyond craft column: an opening should be 'Four sentences, and less than 100 words'; avoid 'paragraph after paragraph of boxed text'.
claims.source: D&D Beyond — Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2019-11-06)
claims.quote: Four sentences, and less than 100 words

claims.claim: A 5e designer describes evolving from verbose 5e style to bullets to boxed text that is 'typically three lines, and never longer than five' because it sped play and set a base tone per room.
claims.source: Revivify Games — What I Value In Adventure Design (2025-03-04)
claims.quote: typically three lines, and never longer than five

claims.claim: Sly Flourish: a read-aloud is a tiny story told in 'less than 250 words'; if editing didn't remove 25% you didn't try; 'Keep it short and keep it powerful.'
claims.source: Sly Flourish — Writing Awesome Read-Aloud Text (Mike Shea, 2010-11-08)
claims.quote: less than 250 words to tell it

claims.claim: Outside introductions, a boxed text with a paragraph break 'isn't already too long by half' is rare; villain dialogue should be broken into ~six-second (one-round) statements.
claims.source: Dungeon Master's Workshop — DM 101: Mastering the Boxed Text (2019-09-27)
claims.quote: isn't already too long by half

claims.claim: Justin Alexander: 'boxed text is often too long'; break 'freeze-frame' text into actionable chunks and stop at the reaction point so players respond before the world moves on.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls (Justin Alexander, 2022-08-01)
claims.quote: boxed text is often too long

claims.claim: Gus L.: a basic room key is five sentences maximum; longer only for puzzles and NPCs — 'no one wants to read a three page key'.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)
claims.quote: no one wants to read a three page key

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch: long read-aloud at each location means 'the players are almost certainly going to be playing with their phones', even when, rarely, the prose is good.
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — (5e) Death in the Wood review (Bryce Lynch, 2019-02-09)

claims.feature: third person over second person in boxed text
claims.claim: Merwin's core fix: 'Move from the second-person point of view to the third person' — 'The bloated corpse of a headless dragon dominates the center of this small clearing' instead of 'As you enter the clearing, you notice…' — so text cannot dictate PC actions or feelings.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
claims.quote: Move from the second-person point of view to the third person

claims.feature: no dictated PC actions or emotions
claims.claim: Merwin's D&D Beyond rules: never 'as you approach' or 'you enter'; never 'stunned', 'terrified', 'heart pounds'; no game-mechanics terms used non-mechanically in boxed text.
claims.source: D&D Beyond — Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2019-11-06)

claims.claim: Alexander names the pitfall 'remote-control text': 'You step forward', 'You smile', or declaring 'the thoughts or feelings' of PCs; show the scene, 'don't tell them how they're reacting to it'.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls (Justin Alexander, 2022-08-01)

claims.claim: Dyson: bad boxed text 'predicts the future for the party (upon approaching…)' or commands behavior ('you stand in shock'); cure is one or two simple sentences or a point-form list.
claims.source: Dyson's Dodecahedron — The Dreaded Boxed Text (Dyson Logos, 2013-09-29)
claims.quote: predicts the future for the party

claims.claim: DM's Workshop argues the opposite of Merwin: shift from third-person objective ('A 200-foot waterfall cascades') to second-person subjective ('You see a majestic waterfall') so the DM addresses the players rather than 'the empty air'.
claims.source: Dungeon Master's Workshop — DM 101: Mastering the Boxed Text (2019-09-27)

verdicts.trueWording: If you're the DM, you get two sentences. Period.
verdicts.note: Raw page via Wayback id_ capture 20210728094635 (live host 403s a bot UA). Page carries verbatim: 'If you're the DM, you get two sentences. Period. Beyond that, your players are stacking dice, talking to each other, or staring off into space' and 'missing the actual data in the boxed text - basic stuff, like room dimensions, how many doors exit the room, and number of monsters.' Dyson explicitly frames it as 'Back in 2005 when Jesse Decker and David Noonan still worked for Wizards of the Coast, they did some awesome hands-on research at the GenCon D&D tables' and links the WotC article. Post dated 29 Sep 2013. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Ditch the boxed text and use your own words
verdicts.note: Post #37 by 'touc', Apr 5, 2025, on page 4. Verbatim on page: 'There's a 2005 WOTC article (archived in criteria comments, Dave Noonan & Jesse Decker)'; the two-sentence block quote; 'DMs who didn't used boxed text had more engagement' (reproduced with the source's own grammatical error); 'DMs with box text are reading it "cold," not having written it in their style nor practiced how it sounds'; and 'Ditch the boxed text and use your own words for the initial description of the room.' The claim's own self-flag stands: this is the forum re-citation, not the upstream WotC article, which I did not fetch.

verdicts.trueWording: 3 to 5 sentences at most and then other details listed
verdicts.note: Both attributions correct on page 4. el-remmen (Moderator Emeritus, #34, Apr 5 2025): 'I find it useful if written well and concisely. 3 to 5 sentences at most and then other details listed to be shared if the party looks closer/investigates/interacts.' - designated quote verbatim, and the 'listed details for closer investigation' limb verbatim too. GM Lent (#31): 'boxed text shouldn't be more than two sentences' - the claim renders this as 'no more than two sentences', a paraphrase of identical meaning, not a verbatim quotation; the limb itself is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Four sentences, and less than 100 words.
verdicts.note: By Shawn Merwin, Nov 6 2019, on dndbeyond.com. Both quoted strings verbatim: under the heading 'A Boxed-Text Opening' the column presents a four-sentence in-media-res opening and comments 'Four sentences, and less than 100 words.'; Tip 2 has 'Nothing slows a game more than paragraph after paragraph of boxed text'. Nuance recorded, not a downgrade: the 100-word figure is stated as a descriptive count of the column's own model opening rather than as an explicit 'should', though the column plainly holds it up as the standard to emulate.

verdicts.trueWording: typically three lines, and never longer than five
verdicts.note: Live host 403s a bare fetch and has no Wayback capture; reached raw on the www. host with full browser headers (HTTP 200). Page dated March 4, 2025. Every limb verbatim: 'the 5e work that I have done was longer form with bolded paragraph leaders and verbose descriptions'; 'So, I evolved and started to work toward the opposite side of the spectrum, focusing on short, bulleted phrases'; 'I introduced boxed text back into my typical formatting'; 'all my boxed text is precise... typically three lines, and never longer than five'; 'In practice, it has sped up play'; 'it allows me, as the designer, to help set a base-level tone for each room'.

verdicts.trueWording: You have a tiny story to tell and less than 250 words
verdicts.note: By Mike (Shea), 8 November 2010. All three fragments verbatim: 'writing good read-aloud text is like writing micro-fiction. You have a tiny story to tell and less than 250 words to tell it'; 'If you didn't edit your read-aloud text and remove 25% of what was there, you didn't try hard enough'; 'Keep it short and keep it powerful.' Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Aside from introductory passages... too long by half
verdicts.note: Under the heading 'Don't Overdo It': 'Aside from introductory passages, it's rare that a boxed text that includes a paragraph break isn't already too long by half. This is especially the case with villain appearances... consider breaking it into statements that can be made in about six seconds - the average length of a round - and drop the phrases in during the fight.' Designated quote verbatim; both limbs, including the six-second/one-round equivalence, verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: I agree that it must be mentioned that boxed text is often too long
verdicts.note: The quotation IS on the page but it is not Justin Alexander's. It appears in the comment section, in the third of three responses, by a commenter named 'Andrew' dated August 2nd, 2022 - 7:13 pm, whose next sentence is 'I also tend to agree with Justin's critiques here', confirming Andrew is not Alexander. The essay body (everything above 'Filed under: Roleplaying Games Comments (3)') contains the string 'too long' zero times. The claim's other limbs ARE Alexander's own: 'what you should do is break it up into actionable chunks', 'What we've identified here is the reaction point', and the rule against letting 'the game world continue to move forward past the reaction point without letting the players react'. Related: the chunk's feature label for this claim, 'attention after three sentences', also traces to a comment - mellonbread, 11:58 am - recalling a lost WotC devblog piece, not to Alexander.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the attribution to Justin Alexander: 'boxed text is often too long' is a reader comment by 'Andrew', not the essay

verdicts.trueWording: Keys longer than five or six sentences can work, with a good editor
verdicts.note: By Gus L., Monday December 19, 2022. The designated quote is verbatim (page: 'No one wants to read a three page key to a single room, written in the style of Undermountian or a 1993 Dungeon Magazine adventure'). But the page does not set five sentences as a maximum. It reads: 'Keys longer than five or six sentences can work, with a good editor, and an attention to ordering their contents, but that's a good basic limit. Longer keys are even needed at times for complex puzzles and npcs, but basic description shouldn't really get beyond a paragraph.' So the figure is five-or-six, framed as a soft 'good basic limit' that longer keys can exceed with editing - and puzzles/NPCs are given as cases where longer is 'even needed at times', not as the sole licensed exception.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'five sentences maximum' and 'longer only for puzzles and NPCs': page says five or six as a soft 'good basic limit' that longer keys can exceed with a good editor

verdicts.trueWording: the players are almost certainly going to be playing with their phones
verdicts.note: Bryce Lynch, '(5e) Death in the Wood', posted February 9, 2019. Body text verbatim: 'There's long read-aloud at the beginning of each location... It's also pretty well written, which I don't think I've said more than three or four times? It does a good job of communicating the social vibe going on. It's still too long and the players are almost certainly going to be playing with their phones, but it's not the overwritten fantasy drivil that is present in most read aloud.' The 'even when, rarely, the prose is good' limb is carried by 'pretty well written, which I don't think I've said more than three or four times'. Sentence is in the review body, not a comment.

verdicts.trueWording: Tip 1. Move from the second-person point of view to the third person.
verdicts.note: Shawn Merwin, Critical Hits, August 27, 2010. Tip 1 heading verbatim. Both example strings verbatim and matching THIS 2010 version rather than the 2019 D&D Beyond rewrite: 'By avoiding the second-person ("As you enter the clearing, you notice the bloated corpse of a headless dragon") and using the third-person ("The bloated corpse of a headless dragon dominates the center of this small clearing")'. The 'actions or feelings' limb is supported in the essay body, not only by inference: 'boxed text can be rife with pitfalls when it assumes character feelings, movements, and actions.'

verdicts.trueWording: avoid 'you' as subject; avoid game mechanical terms used non-mechanically
verdicts.note: Same D&D Beyond column (Merwin, Nov 6 2019). Three of the claim's four quoted strings are verbatim on the page: the bad example carries 'As you approach the tower', Tip 1 rejects 'As you enter the clearing, you notice...', and the mock table dialogue skewers 'your heart pounds' and 'The palpable presence of evil is stunning' / 'You said we were stunned?'. Tip 6 is verbatim: 'Avoid game mechanical terms used in a non-mechanical way', listing 'reaction, action, incapacitated, stunned, frightened, magical'. Graded SUBSTANCE rather than VERBATIM for one word only: 'terrified' does not appear anywhere on the page - the page's words are 'bristle with terror' (in the bad example) and 'frightened' (in Tip 6's mechanical-term list). Tip 1's rationale covers the dictated-emotion limb: avoiding 'you' makes it hard to 'inadvertently include character actions, motivations, feelings, or movements'.

verdicts.trueWording: declaring the thoughts or feelings or (worse yet!) actions of the PCs
verdicts.note: All of this is Alexander's own essay body (above the comment section), unlike claim 101. Section heading 'REMOTE-CONTROL BOXED TEXT'; 'Remote-control boxed text suffers from similar problems (preventing the players from participating), but insidiously goes one step further by declaring the thoughts or feelings or (worse yet!) actions of the PCs'; the two bad examples '"You step forward and return the king's greeting with a deep bow."' and '"As you return to Waterdeep, you smile, thinking fondly of the ale at Trollskull Manor."'; and the cure 'Focus on showing the players the scene and letting them react to it. Don't tell them how they're reacting to it.' Only cosmetic drift: the page's term is 'remote-control boxed text' and the second example's 'you smile' is lowercase mid-sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: predicts the future for the party (upon approaching...)
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture as claim 94. Verbatim: 'On top of which it predicts the future for the party (upon approaching...) instead of leaving that up to them. The only thing it doesn't do that some boxed text insists on doing is truly controlling the PCs with "you stand in shock..." or something similar at the beginning.' The cure limb is verbatim in the closing paragraph: 'reduce it down to one or two SIMPLE sentences. But really, replace it with a point-form list of things seen in the room.' Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: addressed to them instead of the empty air
verdicts.note: Both quoted strings verbatim. Recommendation section: 'don't shy away from shifting text from third-person objective ("A 200-foot waterfall cascades down...") to second-person subjective ("You see a majestic waterfall hundreds of feet in height...") if your players tend to lose focus, as it will help them feel engaged.' Engagement rationale, from the Matthew Mercer passage earlier in the same essay: 'The players are drawn in because the description feels addressed to them instead of the empty air.' The direction of the shift is genuinely the reverse of Merwin's Tip 1 (verified against claims 104/105), though this page never names Merwin. Two nuances recorded, neither an unsupported limb: the two quoted phrases sit in different sections of the one essay, and the advice is conditional ('if your players tend to lose focus') and addressed to a DM adapting published boxed text rather than to a designer writing it.
